text: An agricultural value chain describes how a product moves from a smallholder farm to the final consumer and what each participant along the way does and is paid for. A simplified chain is farmer → local collector/trader → wholesaler → processor → retailer → consumer, though many Cambodian smallholder chains are much shorter (farmer → local trader → processor, or farmer → consumer). The gap between farm-gate price and retail price should not automatically be read as an intermediary's "profit" — participants may be paying for transport, loading, storage, drying, processing, packaging, market fees, spoilage, and business risk. For a smallholder, moving further down the chain (becoming a trader or processor) is not automatically more profitable — it requires working capital, transport, storage, market connections, and willingness to absorb unsold inventory and price risk that a small farm may not have. More realistic value-adding opportunities for a Preah Vihear smallholder are usually smaller: better drying, cleaner produce, accurate weighing, sorting, group aggregation, shared transport, and better records. During the wet season (roughly May–October), the value of a collector/trader who organizes transport and drying tends to increase because farmers face more logistical difficulty doing it themselves; during the dry season (roughly November–April), transport eases but water and heat constraints shift the burden elsewhere in the chain. The useful question for a farmer is not "how do I remove the trader" but "which single activity — drying, sorting, weighing, aggregation, or transport — could I or my farmer group perform more cheaply, while still using the existing buyer network for the parts that are expensive to do alone."
